_meta.description: Plainly's money & banking pack. Plain-English meanings for the jargon on bank, credit-card, loan, and investing sites. Not financial advice; for big decisions, talk to a professional.

apr.simple: the yearly cost of borrowing, shown as a percentage
apr.detailed: Annual Percentage Rate — what a loan or credit card really costs you per year, including interest and most fees. Higher APR means the debt grows faster.
apr.why: A card with 25% APR costs far more to carry a balance on than one at 12%.
apr.next: Compare the APR, not just the monthly payment, when choosing a card or loan.

apy.simple: the yearly return on savings, including compounding
apy.detailed: Annual Percentage Yield — how much a savings account or CD earns in a year once interest-on-interest is counted. Higher is better for you.

interest rate.simple: the percentage charged to borrow, or paid to save
interest rate.detailed: The price of money over time — you pay it on what you borrow, and earn it on what you save.

compound interest.simple: interest that earns interest over time
compound interest.detailed: When your interest itself starts earning interest, money grows faster and faster — great for savings, painful for debt.

principal.simple: the original amount borrowed or invested, before interest
principal.detailed: The core sum — the actual loan amount or deposit — separate from any interest added on top.

credit score.simple: a number that rates how reliably you repay debt
credit score.detailed: A 3-digit score (roughly 300–850) lenders use to judge how risky it is to lend to you. Higher usually means better rates.
credit score.why: It affects whether you're approved for loans and cards, and how much interest you'll pay.

credit report.simple: a detailed record of your borrowing history
credit report.detailed: A file showing your loans, cards, payment history, and debts. Your credit score is calculated from it.
credit report.next: You can check it for free periodically and dispute mistakes.

credit limit.simple: the most you're allowed to borrow on a card

credit utilization.simple: how much of your available credit you're using
credit utilization.detailed: The share of your credit limit you've spent. Keeping it low (often under 30%) tends to help your credit score.

minimum payment.simple: the smallest amount you must pay this month to stay current
minimum payment.why: Paying only the minimum keeps the account in good standing but lets interest pile up on the rest.
minimum payment.next: Pay more than the minimum whenever you can to cut interest.

statement balance.simple: what you owed at the end of the billing cycle
statement balance.detailed: The total from your last statement. Paying this in full by the due date usually means no interest.

available balance.simple: the money you can actually spend right now
available balance.detailed: Your balance minus holds and pending charges — often less than the 'current balance' shown.

overdraft.simple: spending more than you have in your account
overdraft.detailed: When a payment goes through even though your balance can't cover it, leaving you negative — usually with a fee.
overdraft.why: Overdraft fees add up fast and can trigger more of them.

ach.detailed: Automated Clearing House — the network behind direct deposit, autopay, and moving money between banks. Usually free but takes 1–3 days.

wire transfer.simple: a fast, usually same-day bank transfer
wire transfer.detailed: A direct electronic transfer of funds between banks — quick and hard to reverse, so it's a common target for scams.
wire transfer.why: Wires are often irreversible; if you're tricked into sending one, the money may be gone.

routing number.simple: a 9-digit code that identifies your bank
routing number.detailed: The number that tells the system which bank an account belongs to, used for transfers and direct deposit.

direct deposit.simple: having pay or benefits sent straight to your account

autopay.simple: automatic recurring payments from your account
autopay.why: Handy for avoiding late fees, but watch the balance so autopay doesn't overdraw you.

late fee.simple: a charge for paying after the due date

annual fee.simple: a yearly charge just for having a card or account

cash advance.simple: borrowing cash against your credit card — usually expensive
cash advance.detailed: Taking cash from a credit card. It typically has a higher rate than purchases and starts charging interest immediately, with a fee.
cash advance.why: Cash advances are one of the costliest ways to use a card.

balance transfer.simple: moving debt from one card to another, often at lower interest
balance transfer.detailed: Shifting what you owe onto a new card — sometimes at 0% for a while — to pay it down faster. Usually has a transfer fee.

grace period.simple: time to pay before interest or penalties kick in
grace period.detailed: The window (often around 21–25 days on cards) where paying in full means you owe no interest.

refinance.simple: replace a loan with a new one on better terms
refinance.detailed: Take out a new loan to pay off an old one — usually to get a lower rate or smaller payment.

escrow.simple: money held by a neutral third party until conditions are met
escrow.detailed: Funds parked with a middleman — common in home buying, where taxes and insurance are collected monthly and paid on your behalf.

mortgage.simple: a loan used to buy a home, with the home as security
mortgage.detailed: A long-term loan for property; if you stop paying, the lender can take the home.

amortization.simple: paying off a loan in steady scheduled payments over time
amortization.detailed: How a loan balance shrinks with each payment; early on, more of each payment goes to interest than to principal.

collateral.simple: something you pledge that the lender can take if you don't repay
collateral.detailed: An asset (like a car or house) backing a loan; default and the lender can seize it.

down payment.simple: the upfront cash you pay toward a big purchase
down payment.detailed: The portion you pay yourself (e.g. on a house or car); the rest is financed with a loan.

principal balance.simple: how much of the original loan you still owe

fdic.simple: government insurance that protects bank deposits
fdic.detailed: The FDIC insures money in U.S. banks (up to a limit per depositor) so you don't lose it if the bank fails.

chargeback.simple: reversing a card charge by disputing it with your bank
chargeback.detailed: When you ask your card issuer to undo a payment — for fraud or a problem with a purchase — and get the money back.

inflation.simple: the gradual rise in prices that shrinks what money buys

capital gains.simple: the profit when you sell something for more than you paid
capital gains.detailed: The gain on selling an investment or asset; it's often taxed.

dividend.simple: a share of a company's profits paid to its investors

index fund.simple: an investment that tracks a whole market instead of picking stocks
index fund.detailed: A fund that mirrors a market index (like the S&P 500), giving broad, low-cost diversification.

etf.simple: a basket of investments you can buy like a single stock
etf.detailed: Exchange-Traded Fund — a bundle of assets that trades on an exchange, often used for low-cost, diversified investing.

portfolio.simple: the full collection of your investments

diversification.simple: spreading money across many investments to lower risk
diversification.detailed: Not putting all your eggs in one basket, so one bad investment doesn't sink everything.

401k.simple: a workplace retirement savings account with tax perks
401k.detailed: An employer-based plan where you save for retirement pre-tax, often with a company match — free money you don't want to leave on the table.

ira.simple: a personal retirement account with tax advantages
ira.detailed: Individual Retirement Account — a tax-favored account you open yourself to save for retirement (Traditional or Roth).

vesting.simple: gradually earning full ownership of something over time
vesting.detailed: Common with employer match or stock: you fully own it only after staying long enough. Leave early and you may forfeit the unvested part.
